text: How long will this take to run is a question every stakeholder asks, and the honest answer is almost entirely about queue depth, not computation. This lesson turns that into an actual latency budget you can set and defend before a project starts.

We'll build a per-stage latency budget from real measured numbers, see which single lever is actually worth pulling, set a realistic end-to-end deadline, and learn how to communicate that budget honestly to a non-technical stakeholder.

Here's the same per-stage breakdown from Chapter 3, read as a budget instead of a measurement. Queue wait is ninety-nine point zero seven percent of total time. Shaving the twelve-millisecond classical prep step in half saves zero point zero one six percent of total latency — not worth a single engineering hour. Reducing queue wait, by switching devices or by batching, is where all the real leverage is.

And queue depth is a real, checkable property — right here on a real device list. Over a hundred fifty iterations with no batching, that thirty-eight-second average queue wait adds up to roughly ninety-six minutes. That's the number to put in a project plan, not the forty-millisecond QPU execution time alone.

Here's the provider's own real diagram of the stages a latency budget is actually built from: submit, queue, translate, run, retrieve. Batching changes the shape of this budget dramatically — not by reducing queue wait itself, but by reducing how many times you pay it.

And here's where the real timestamps behind all of this live — a real task detail page. A latency budget should be presented as a range tied to an explicit assumption: based on this device's observed queue wait, expect roughly this long, but a busier day could push it well past that. That framing names the dominant variable explicitly, instead of treating any deviation as evidence the estimate was wrong.
Next lesson covers the one knob in a hybrid workflow that directly trades real money for statistical precision, on a well-defined mathematical curve: shot count.
